facts.statehood_note: North Dakota and South Dakota were admitted on the same day. Which was signed first was not recorded, so North Dakota is counted as the 39th state because it comes first in the alphabet.
facts.nickname: The Peace Garden State (official since 1957); also called the Flickertail State and the Roughrider State
facts.motto: Liberty and Union, Now and Forever, One and Inseparable (from a speech by Daniel Webster). The state's Latin motto is "Serit ut alteri saeclo prosit" ("One sows for the benefit of another age").
facts.name_origin: Named for the Dakota and Sioux peoples. "Dakota" is a word meaning "friends" or "allies."

government.legislature: North Dakota Legislative Assembly, which meets in the State Capitol in Bismarck for up to 80 days every other year (odd-numbered years)
government.chambers: North Dakota Senate (47 senators) and North Dakota House of Representatives (94 representatives): 47 districts, each electing one senator and two representatives to 4-year terms. Voters in 2022 limited lawmakers to two 4-year terms in each house.
government.executive: Governor (4-year term). The lieutenant governor serves as President of the Senate and votes only to break a tie. It takes two-thirds of both houses to override a governor's veto.
government.courts: North Dakota Supreme Court (5 justices, elected to staggered 10-year terms). The court began with 4 justices under the 1889 constitution and grew to 5 in 1915.
government.local: 53 counties, plus cities and townships. The state's five tribal nations are sovereign: each has its own constitution, tribal council, chairperson, and courts on its reservation.
government.constitution: The North Dakota Constitution was written at the 1889 constitutional convention, when the state was created; it set up the state courts, and the convention also debated votes for women.
government.kid_line: "All individuals are by nature equally free and independent and have certain inalienable rights" (Article I, Section 1)

long_ago.about: The Mandan moved from the Minnesota and Iowa area to the Plains and reached North Dakota around 1000 A.D. They lived in earthlodge villages along the Missouri River and farmed corn, beans, squash, and sunflowers.

The Hidatsa moved from central Minnesota to the Devils Lake area and then joined the Mandan on the Missouri River around 1600. Hidatsa women built and owned the earthlodges, which could be up to 40 feet across, and managed the gardens.

The Arikara once lived across lands reaching from the Gulf of Mexico through Kansas, Nebraska, and South Dakota and later moved up the Missouri River. In 1862 they joined the Mandan and Hidatsa at Like-a-Fishhook Village.

Yanktonai (Ihanktonwana) Dakota and Hunkpapa and Sihasapa Lakota lived across much of the state. By the early 1800s Lakota life centered on the horse and the buffalo, and families lived in tipis all year.

The Ojibwe and Cree lived in the northeast. In the Turtle Mountains, Plains Ojibwe and Métis families hunted buffalo twice a year to make pemmican, gathered wild foods, and trapped furs for trade, and they made the homemade Red River Cart.

today.nation: Mandan, Hidatsa, and Arikara Nation (Three Affiliated Tribes)
today.about: Headquartered in New Town on the Fort Berthold Indian Reservation along the Missouri River; 17,592 enrolled members as of April 2025.

Headquartered in Fort Yates; its reservation of about 2.3 million acres crosses the North Dakota and South Dakota line along the Missouri River and is home to Dakota (Yanktonai) and Lakota (Hunkpapa and Sihasapa) people.

Once called the Devils Lake Sioux; headquartered in Fort Totten, with a reservation of about 405 square miles, mostly in Benson County and bordering Devils Lake; Dakota chiefs signed a treaty there in 1867.

today.nation: Turtle Mountain Band of Chippewa Indians
today.about: Ojibwe (Anishinaabe) and Métis nation headquartered in Belcourt, Rolette County, on a reservation set up in 1882; about 33,276 enrolled members (2024), speaking English, Ojibwe, and Michif.

A Dakota nation headquartered at Agency Village, South Dakota; its Lake Traverse Reservation extends into southeastern North Dakota, so it is one of the five tribal nations the North Dakota Indian Affairs Commission works with.

first_peoples.today_note: All five tribal nations are federally recognized and are located at least partly in North Dakota (the Sisseton Wahpeton Oyate is based in South Dakota). They are sovereign, so state law does not govern them on their reservations, and a tribal chair holds the same rank as the governor. The North Dakota Indian Affairs Commission helps the state and the tribes work together.

Whitestone Hill State Historic Site, Dickey County, with a monument to the Dakota and Lakota people killed there in 1863

history.event: The Mandan reach what is now North Dakota and build farming villages along the Missouri River.

Hidatsa, Mandan, and later Arikara families live in five villages near the Knife and Missouri Rivers, with up to 3,500 people. They trade across a network reaching from the Gulf Coast to the Rocky Mountains.
French explorer La Vérendrye leads the first recorded European expedition into the area.
A smallpox outbreak kills many Hidatsa and Mandan people.
The Lewis and Clark Expedition spends the winter at Fort Mandan near the Knife River villages. Sakakawea, a Shoshone woman living among the Hidatsa, joins the expedition.
The American Fur Company builds Fort Union, a fur trading post, near where the Yellowstone River meets the Missouri, at the request of the Assiniboine Nation.
Another smallpox outbreak cuts the Knife River villages' population by about half. In 1845 survivors move to Like-a-Fishhook Village, their last traditional earthlodge village.
The Fort Laramie Treaty of 1851 is signed; the MHA Nation's government traces its start to this treaty.
The U.S. creates Dakota Territory. President Abraham Lincoln appoints its first governor, and the 1862 Homestead Act soon draws many settlers.

After the 1862 U.S.-Dakota War in Minnesota, General Alfred Sully's troops attack a camp of Yanktonai, Dakota, Hunkpapa, and Sihasapa people at Whitestone Hill. Many men, women, and children are killed or captured, and the camp's food and tipis are destroyed.
Sully's army attacks Lakota and Yanktonai people in the Killdeer Mountains.
Dakota chiefs sign a treaty with the United States; Wahpeton, Sisseton, and Yanktonai bands are living at Spirit Lake.
Women in Dakota Territory win the right to vote on school issues.
North Dakota becomes the 39th state. At the constitutional convention, Linda Warfel Slaughter leads the push for women's right to vote.

trailblazers.name: Sakakawea (Sacagawea)
trailblazers.group: Shoshone woman living among the Hidatsa
trailblazers.text: Sakakawea was a Shoshone captive living in a Hidatsa village on the Knife River when the Lewis and Clark Expedition wintered nearby. She and her baby son traveled with the expedition; she translated, and nations they met saw a woman and child as a sign the group was not a war party.

trailblazers.name: Buffalo Bird Woman (Waheenee)
trailblazers.text: Born near the Knife River, she moved to Like-a-Fishhook Village as a small child. From 1907 to 1918 she taught researcher Gilbert Wilson how Hidatsa women grew corn, beans, squash, and sunflowers, and the book Buffalo Bird Woman's Garden (1917) still teaches traditional Hidatsa farming.

trailblazers.name: Sitting Bull
trailblazers.text: Sitting Bull, a leader of the Hunkpapa Lakota, surrendered to the U.S. Army at Fort Buford in 1881. Hunkpapa people are part of the Standing Rock Sioux Tribe today, and the tribe runs Sitting Bull College.

trailblazers.name: Linda Warfel Slaughter
trailblazers.text: A Bismarck woman who led the fight for women's right to vote at North Dakota's 1889 constitutional convention. Women in the state won partial voting rights in 1917 and full voting rights through the 19th Amendment in 1920.

trailblazers.name: Era Bell Thompson
trailblazers.group: Black American woman, journalist and author
trailblazers.text: She moved with her family to a farm near Driscoll in 1917 and set state women's track records at the University of North Dakota. She became co-managing editor and then international editor of Ebony magazine, and her book American Daughter tells of growing up in North Dakota. She received the state's Rough Rider Award in 1976.

trailblazers.name: Dr. Anne H. Carlsen
trailblazers.text: Born without hands or feet, she earned a Ph.D. in 1949 and in 1950 became superintendent of the Crippled Children's School in Jamestown, which became the nationally known Anne Carlsen Center for Children. She received the Rough Rider Award in 1966.

Little Missouri Badlands in the west

White Butte (about 3,506 feet), the highest point

geography.regions: North Dakota has the flat Red River Valley in the east, the Drift Prairie and Missouri Plateau in the middle, and the Badlands west of the Missouri River.

ecosystems.name: Little Missouri Badlands
ecosystems.about: Theodore Roosevelt National Park protects 70,446 acres of badlands, prairie, and river woods, with bison, elk, pronghorn, bighorn sheep, a free-ranging horse herd, and 1,235 acres of black-tailed prairie dog towns.

ecosystems.name: Missouri River valley
ecosystems.about: Rich river soil let Hidatsa and Mandan women grow corn, beans, squash, and sunflowers for hundreds of years, and cottonwood posts held up their earthlodges.

ecosystems.name: Red River Valley prairie
ecosystems.about: The flat valley is the floor of old glacial Lake Agassiz, which makes it very flat and slow to drain when spring snow melts.

science.weather: Cold winters and warm summers. Winter storms (blizzards, ice storms, extreme cold), spring river floods, tornadoes, and wildfires are the main hazards. Langdon once stayed below 0°F for 41 days in a row (1935 to 1936), and in April 1997 the Red River flooded most of Grand Forks.
science.resources: Farming is the largest industry, and North Dakota leads the nation in durum wheat. Oil from the Bakken formation (first found near Tioga in 1951) and large lignite coal reserves are also important.
science.highlight: The Red River of the North flows north toward Canada. In spring, melting snow in the south runs into ice that has not melted farther north, and the flat old lakebed drains slowly, which is why the 1997 flood reached about 54 feet at Grand Forks and more than 50,000 people had to leave.

g3_ss.title: North Dakota's Communities and Government
g3_ss.plan: Map Bismarck, Fargo, and the 53 counties; meet the Legislative Assembly (47 senators, 94 representatives), the governor, and the 5-justice Supreme Court; learn that the five tribal nations have their own governments.

g3_ss.title: North Dakota's First Peoples
g3_ss.plan: Earthlodge life of the Mandan, Hidatsa, and Arikara; Dakota and Lakota buffalo life; Turtle Mountain Ojibwe and Métis; meet the five tribal nations today.

g3_ss.title: North Dakota Trailblazers
g3_ss.plan: Short biographies of Buffalo Bird Woman, Sakakawea, Era Bell Thompson, and Anne Carlsen.

g45_ss.title: North Dakota's First Nations
g45_ss.plan: The Knife River villages (c. 1525 to 1845), Hidatsa women as farmers and lodge owners, trade networks, and the smallpox outbreaks of 1780 and 1837.

g45_ss.title: Explorers, Fur Traders, and Treaties
g45_ss.plan: La Vérendrye (1738), Lewis and Clark and Sakakawea at Fort Mandan (1804 to 1805), Fort Union (1828), and the Fort Laramie Treaty of 1851.

g45_ss.title: Dakota Territory to Statehood
g45_ss.plan: Dakota Territory (1861), Whitestone Hill (1863) and Killdeer Mountain (1864) told from the Dakota and Lakota side, reservations, women's suffrage, and statehood in 1889.

g3_sci.title: Prairie Dogs and Bison of the Badlands
g3_sci.plan: Animals of Theodore Roosevelt National Park and how prairie dog towns and grazing bison shape the grassland.

g3_sci.title: Winter on the Plains
g3_sci.plan: Blizzards, extreme cold, and staying safe; the 41 days below zero at Langdon.

g3_sci.title: Three Sisters and Sunflowers
g3_sci.plan: Plant corn, beans, squash, and sunflowers the way Buffalo Bird Woman described, and observe how they grow.

g45_sci.title: The River That Flows North
g45_sci.plan: Why the Red River floods: north-flowing water, ice jams, a flat old lakebed, and the 1997 Grand Forks flood.

g45_sci.title: Glaciers and Lake Agassiz
g45_sci.plan: How an ice-age lake left the flat, fertile Red River Valley; compare with the Badlands and Missouri Plateau.

g45_sci.title: Energy from Underground
g45_sci.plan: Lignite coal and Bakken oil: what they are, where they are found, and how energy development affects air and land in the Badlands.
